title: Backwards Compatibility Checks and Publication Automation Playbook
body:
Purpose:
This playbook defines a pragmatic, test-first approach to publishing Terraform modules for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) that minimizes customer disruption. It focuses on automating pre-publish compatibility checks, tagging and registry metadata practices, and a clear checklist for breaking changes and deprecation windows.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to all tf modules published to our internal module registry used by Private and Dedicated customers.
- Assumes consumers pin to module versions (recommended) but often run periodic upgrades via infra pipelines.
- Covers semantic compatibility tiers, automated test suites, publishing scripts, and communication templates.

Compatibility classification (quick reference):
- NON-BREAKING: Additive fields, optional inputs, new resources behind flags, lower-risk fixes.
- GREY-AREA: Changes that alter default behavior (e.g., change default value), but preserve old codepaths via a compatibility flag for at least 2 releases.
- BREAKING: Removal/rename of inputs/outputs, change in resource lifecycle, or config schema incompatible with previous state. Requires deprecation window + migration guide.

Pre-publish automated checks (CI job: module-backcompat):
1) Static schema check: compare module input/output schemas between latest-released tag and candidate branch. Fail on missing items unless migration annotated.
2) State import test: run terraform init/apply in disposable env using recorded minimal example state from last release, then terraform plan against candidate. Any plan that shows resource destroy/recreate by default is flagged.
3) Integration smoke: run our onprem smoke harness (lightweight provisioning + apply/destroy) for supported providers (aws, gcp, azure, k8s). Timebox 30m.
4) Examples and pinned-tests: re-run all example folders pinned to previous stable versions to validate no drift.
5) Upgrade path simulation: run terraform apply with previous module version, then terraform init -upgrade to candidate, then plan. Capture diffs and generate 'upgrade-delta' artifact.

Publishing automation: recommended pipeline (release pipeline: release-module.yml)
- Trigger: merge to main with release label (release/module).
- Steps: 1) module-backcompat CI (must pass) 2) bump-version utility (see tagging below) 3) generate release notes (from CHANGELOG + migration notes) 4) publish to internal registry via registry-publish script (atomic) 5) smoke canary promotion (promote to staging consumers list) 6) notify subscribers (email/slack + PR to docs).

Tagging and versioning conventions (machine-friendly):
- Version: <major>.<minor>.<patch>-<buildmeta> (buildmeta optional). We prefer simple semver but use a pre-release tag for experimental changes, e.g., 2.4.0-alpha1.
- Release branches: release/x.y used for emergency patching.
- Tag annotation: include 'compat:non-breaking' | 'compat:grey' | 'compat:breaking' and 'migration:link=<URL>' fields in annotated tag message.
- Registry metadata: include a file module.metadata.json at root with fields: compatible_with (list of older major tags as strings), minimum_provider_versions, deprecation_window_days. Publishing script reads this and refuses breaking publishes without deprecation_window >= 30.

Breaking-change policy checklist (required when compat:breaking):
- [ ] Confirm design review with product/security (link PR and design doc).
- [ ] Populate migration guide in docs/ with examples (older -> new).
- [ ] Add a compatibility flag where feasible to gate new behavior for 2 minor releases.
- [ ] Update module.metadata.json.deprecation_window_days >= 30.
- [ ] Run a customer-impact sweep: list infra repos that import the module (search by registry path), compile a subscriber list.
- [ ] Create JIRA ticket with migration tasks and estimated effort per major customer.
- [ ] Schedule coordinated publish + webhook to notify private deployments team and account owners.

Examples: upgrade simulation snippet (CI step):
- git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-examples.git && cd examples/module-consumer-basic && tfenv use 1.4.6 && terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform apply -auto-approve -var "module_source=registry.internal/redwood/tf/example//?ref=v2.3.1" && terraform plan -var "module_source=registry.internal/redwood/tf/example//?ref=v2.4.0" -out=upgrade.plan 
- Convert plan to human diff and attach as artifact.

Release notes template (for automation-generated drafts):
- Title: Module: <name> v<version>
- Summary: Short summary of changes and risk level (non-breaking/grey/breaking).
- Migration notes: Step-by-step if needed.
- Known impacted consumers: list from repo search.
- Rollback steps: pin prior module version + example config.

Canary & rollout guidance for Private deployments:
- Canary group: 5–10 internal customer tenants (or staging orgs). If onprem customers opt-in, coordinate with success.
- Monitor window: 72 hours for config drift, 7 days for latent state defects.
- Automated rollback: publish script keeps prior version available and triggers alert with /rollback playbook attached.

Communication templates (brief):
- Slack alert (ops-channel): "[module publish] <module> v<ver> (compat:<level>) published to registry. Canary started: <canary-list>. Migration doc: <link>"
- Customer email (for breaking): short heading, reason, migration steps with example, expected timeline, contact person.

Non-technical mitigations and checklist items:
- Provide a compatibility test harness repo customers can run locally. Keep it lightweight and documented.
- Offer a migration office-hours slot the week after any breaking publish.
- Maintain a rolling 'Affected-consumers' table in Confluence with contact and upgrade priority.

Housekeeping & governance:
- Any breaking publish must be approved by at least two senior engineers and the private deployments PM. Approval recorded as a GitHub review + JIRA approval.
- Every month: run a 'registry health' job to detect untagged modules, modules without metadata, and modules with no compatibility annotations. Generate a remediation backlog.

Open questions & next steps (work-in-progress):
- Decide enforced minimum deprecation window for grey-area changes (proposal: 60 days).
- Implement a small python utility that diff-summarizes state import deltas into a human-readable migration checklist.
- Pilot the release pipeline with one module group and gather failure modes.

Appendix: quick failure scenarios and responses
- CI flags state-destroy -> block publish and open dev ticket; recommended path: add compatibility flag or migration resource.
- Post-publish latent destroy observed in canary -> immediately cut new patch with guard (if possible) and notify customers; otherwise coordinate rollback and support.

Owner notes:
- This is intentionally prescriptive but lightweight: goal is to shift risk left with automated checks and to formalize communication only for the highest-risk changes.
- Feedback requested from module owners and SREs: does the import-state simulation cover our main failure modes?
